title: Landline not working? Simple steps to take before contacting customer service
summary: Landline not working? Check phone jacks, cords, handsets and batteries, and learn when to contact your service provider.
body_markdown:
Oh, no. The landline house phone isn’t working. You aren’t technical, and you’ve got your hands full with the kids.


Wait. Maybe that’s the problem: the home phone line isn’t working because a child pulled the line out of the jack! Or maybe Dex did it. That dog is mischievous. Or maybe it just broke. There are many possibilities and you’re not an expert.


We are. Below, we’ll go through what you can do yourself before having to worry about calling customer service.


## ET, check phone!


ET the extraterrestrial didn’t have to worry about his phone not ringing, but when you have no dial tone here on Earth, that’s frustrating. While it’s true there are[fewer landline phones](https://www.ooma.com/blog/changes-in-number-of-homes-with-landlines/) today due to the proliferation of smartphones and the[copper sunset](https://www.ooma.com/blog/business/att-copper-shutdown-pots-phaseout-2025-2029/) (phasing out of traditional landline infrastructure), your landline is still plenty smart enough for you—as long as it’s working.


So let’s see what the problem might be. Chances are, it’s something super simple that you’ll be able to fix in just a few minutes.


## Check the phone line


Does your house have more than one landline? Is the phone not ringing on only one device? It’s likely a jack problem. (Did you start humming, “[Hit the road, Jack!](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-aUMOgjX-nw) ” just now? We thought so.)


Here’s how to check your home phone line: unplug the non-working phone, and plug this phone into another phone jack in the house. Make sure you use the same phone cord.


If you have a dial tone now, the phone jack was the issue. Problem identified.


If you still don’t have a dial tone, we can’t blame the jack. Either the phone is broken, or the cord is the problem. Hello, Dex, you’ve got a hangdog look there, buddy.


Try swapping out the phone cord for a new one on your existing setup. Got a dial tone now? Good work. It’s your decision as to whether and when to let Dex off the hook.


If the phone *still* doesn’t work, it might be time for a new phone.


## My phone is not ringing


What if you have no dial tone at all on any phone? Well, speaking of “off the hook,” this may be precisely the problem: somebody left the phone receiver off the hook. It’s easy to think the handset is fully in its cradle when it’s not.


When a handset is left off the hook for more than a brief period, there will be a busy signal, followed by high-pitched, timed warning sounds. If the phone remains off the hook indefinitely, it leads to a circuit lockout: the exchange eventually disconnects the active signal on that circuit until the handset is placed back on its cradle.


So if you have no dial tone on any phone at all? Don’t panic! Make sure all handsets are securely in their cradles and wait a minute for the system to reset.


If you have a cordless system and the base has lost its connection, what you need to do is unplug each phone in the house, one at a time. Wait 30 seconds, plug them back in and then check for a dial tone.


## Charge it!


Or maybe your non-working phone is out of juice. Have you checked the battery lately? If your landline isn’t working, it might be because the battery isn’t charging.


Here’s how to check the phone battery. First, make sure it was sitting on the cradle correctly. Sometimes we can accidentally place the phone in the cradle a little wrong and it won’t charge.


If that doesn’t do the trick, then remove the handset battery cover, clean the battery and battery cavity with a dry cloth, and see if it charges now. If so, presto! You’ve just fixed your phone.


If it still doesn’t work, the battery might need replacing. Check your manufacturer’s guide for steps on how to replace your phone’s battery.


## Disconnect from the landline


Okay, we know this is the age of connectivity, but if you haven’t yet fixed the issue, we’re going to ask you to disconnect: unplug the answering machine, fax, modem, and anything else you have plugged into the wall jacks.


Why disconnect? This process helps identify whether the issue lies with the phone itself, the wiring, or another connected device that may be causing interference.


Now let’s test the “problem” phone again.


Got a dial tone now? Then the fault lies with one of the disconnected devices. You’re becoming a super-sleuth. Still no dial tone? Then it’s time to leave the house. Here’s what we mean.


## Test the exterior NID


It’s time to go outside. Take a working corded phone from the house with you. We’re going to visit…the phone box. (Note: if this is a newer home, there may not be a landline phone box! If not, you’ll have to call a repair technician. However, if the house was built back when landlines were standard, the odds are good you have one, and you can continue to troubleshoot yourself.)


Known formally as the Network Interface Device (NID), the phone box is typically a small, gray or beige weatherproof plastic box, usually mounted on an outside wall, labeled with a telephone symbol. But it might be in your basement, if you have one, or in the garage.


Once you find the phone service box, open it up. You might have to unscrew it first. Then, unplug the modular connection plug, which should look like a latch. You should see an area where your phone lines plug into the NID. Plug the test phone directly into the test jack.


If you can hear a dial tone here, the line itself is fine, but there’s a problem with the home’s wiring. You’ll have to call a repair technician. If there’s no dial tone at the test jack, the problem may be with the outside line or your provider’s service. Contact your service provider.


On the bright side: look how much you were able to accomplish on your own! Great job. Now you can reach out to your service provider and request a repair, ASAP. After all, you’ve got children to take care of. You can’t be in a house where the phone’s not ringing.


## Landline not working consistently?


Okay, let’s say you’ve resolved the dial tone issue. But there’s another annoying problem: the phone drops calls, or the person you’re talking to sounds far away, or under water.


Once you’ve tested the jacks, batteries, phone cords and connected devices and determined none of these is the cause, the static or dropped calls are likely coming from the outside line or your provider’s service. This is a job for your service provider.


## Landline house phone alternatives


We understand how dealing with this type of issue can be aggravating. Fortunately, today there are landline options that combine traditional landline security with modern convenience.


One of the best[landline alternatives](https://www.ooma.com/blog/home-phone/best-landline-alternative/) is VoIP: Voice over Internet Protocol. VoIP technology allows you to place phone calls through an internet connection, rather than using copper-wire phone lines that have been around for nearly 150 years and are being discontinued.


This is also good news considering how[phone bills are rising](https://www.ooma.com/blog/home-phone/landline-home-phone-is-getting-more-expensive/) . In the age of smartphones, when almost everybody wants a phone in their palm or pocket, landline phones are not only becoming less popular; their aging copper-wire infrastructure is fading into the sunset. And fewer customers for an older phone system mean higher costs.


With VoIP, you can call anyone, anywhere, just like you would with a traditional home phone. You can even make phone calls from your laptop or desktop computer!


VoIP is also a much more[affordable home phone service](https://www.ooma.com/home-phone/cheap-home-phone-service/) —and makes it easy for emergency responders to find your house by forwarding your address to 911 dispatchers. Also, you can keep your original phone number when you switch to a VoIP phone system.


So before that old landline house phone fades into the copper sunset, consider upgrading your home phone line to Ooma Telo. Everyone will be happier, and Jack will never need to hit the road again.
